title: Comparative practice: two poems about leaving home
stem:
Paper 2 is written on two literary works you have studied. To practise comparative thinking, compare these two short original poems.

POEM 1 — Suitcase
My mother packed the kitchen in a case:
the cardamom, the ladle, Sunday's taste.
She folded up our language with the sheets
and smoothed it flat, as if it might not keep.

POEM 2 — Arrivals
nobody here
says my name right
so I say it
louder

at the airport my father
looked at the signs
like a man reading
his own sentence

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare how the two poems use form and structure to present the experience of migration.
markscheme: Poem 1: regular quatrain with rhyming couplets (case/taste, sheets/keep half-rhyme) suggests order, care and the attempt to contain loss
Poem 2: free verse, short lines, no punctuation or capitals suggest fragmentation and uncertainty
Poem 2 isolates 'louder' on its own line: assertion of identity as defiance
Poem 1's metaphor of 'folding' language like sheets presents culture as something portable but fragile
Poem 2's ambiguity in 'sentence' (grammar/judicial punishment) presents arrival as a trial
comparative point: Poem 1 focuses on preserving heritage before departure; Poem 2 on struggling for recognition after arrival
both use family figures (mother, father) to channel collective experience
comparison is integrated with precise references to both poems

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Discuss which poem presents identity as more under threat, with reference to both texts.
markscheme: Poem 1: 'as if it might not keep' – fear that language will spoil/be lost
Poem 2: mispronounced name shows identity misrecognised by others
father's 'sentence' suggests powerlessness before an unfamiliar system
Poem 2's speaker responds with agency ('say it / louder'), complicating the threat
reaches a reasoned judgement that weighs both poems
